newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Truce fails to halt Bangladesh tribal violence.
newsitem.headline: Truce fails to halt Bangladesh tribal violence.

text.p: Tribal rebels in Bangladesh's southeastern Chittagong Hill Tracts resorted to violence more often during times of truce than when officially fighting the army, military officials said on Tuesday.
"They are more active in truce than any other time," one official said of Shanti Bahini (peace force) guerrillas in the 5,500 square-mile (14,200 sq-km) Hill Tracts, bordering India and Burma.
During the current truce that expires on September 30, the Shantis killed 30 Bengali-speaking settlers and ambushed soldiers more than a dozen times, the official told Reuters.
The settlers were killed on September 10. Most of the victims had been beheaded.
The rebels also laid traps for police and other securitymen, officials said. "Casualties occurred during the exchanges and arms were seized," the Hill Tracts official said on Tuesday.

He said the government was still hoping to renew the truce "to give peace another try" and to encourage thousands of Bangladeshi tribal families who fled to the Indian state of Tripura to return home.
"The killing of the 30 settlers...has reinforced fears among both tribals and non-tribals of a further flare up of ethnic tension," said the official, who declined to be identified.
The Shantis, mostly members of the Hill Tract's largest Chakma tribe, took up arms in 1973 after Bangladesh rejected their demand for autonomy.
The rebels later asked the government to pull out some 300,000 Bengali-speaking settlers from the hill and forest region, which they consider their tribal homeland.
Bangladesh rejected both the demands but has renewed a truce more than 10 times since 1992 and offered several amnesties.

"But nothing has been achieved," another Hill Tracts official told Reuters on Tuesday. "Every time we extend the truce, the rebels use it for intensifying attacks on civilians and securitymen, and to collect tolls at gunpoint."
More than 1,200 rebels, 1,000 tribals, 5,000 non-tribals and 500 securitymen have been killed in the 23-year insurgency, according to official figures.
Unofficial sources put the casualty toll higher.

More than 45,000 tribespeople have fled to northeast India over the last five or six years to escape the insurgency. Some 5,000 were repatriated in 1994 and more than 2,000 others managed to return on their own, Hill Tracts officials said.
Military sources in the Hill Tracts said the Shantis were now inducting new recruits from among young tribesmen, apparently preparing for a new onslaught against the army.
